headline: Google Keep integrates Gemini voice-to-list for automatic checklist creation
summary: The new AI-powered feature accurately transcribes natural speech and automatically formats it into editable checklists, significantly streamlining note-taking for busy users. It requires a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription.
details: Google Keep has integrated Gemini's AI-powered voice feature, transforming how users create checklists and notes. This new functionality accurately transcribes natural speech and automatically formats it into structured, editable checkbox lists, saving significant time and frustration. Accessing this feature requires a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription.

Previously, Google Keep's voice notes offered basic transcription that often required manual editing and formatting into lists. Gemini's integration now understands conversational-style recordings, converting them directly into organized lists without user intervention. This streamlines the process for busy individuals.

Users can initiate list creation by speaking to Gemini directly from their home screen, which often yields more accurate results than traditional Keep voice notes. This method also bypasses Keep's 30-second recording limit, allowing for longer, more comprehensive dictations.

For example, a prompt like "I need milk, Nespresso pods, ground coffee, sugar. Add pasta, pasta sauce, Tabasco sauce, and Cholula hot sauce to the list" is accurately processed. Gemini identifies all items and creates a proper checklist in Keep.

While highly effective, the feature's accuracy can be affected by noisy surroundings or extremely fast speech. Despite these minor limitations, the integration is recommended for users seeking to enhance their efficiency in managing tasks and shopping lists.

headline_marked: [[MCP was a mistake]]: 200,000 tokens prove protocol design burns AI context windows
headline: MCP was a mistake: 200,000 tokens prove protocol design burns AI context windows
summary: Benchmarking reveals the MCP protocol injects over 100,000 tokens of JSON schemas into LLM context windows on connection, costing users significantly before any interaction.
details: OpenClaw founder Peter Steinberger calls MCP a "mistake," a sentiment echoed by YC's CEO. Despite 97 million downloads and backing from major AI players, new benchmarks reveal a critical flaw in the protocol's design.

Connecting just 10 popular MCP servers to a token counter showed over 100,000 tokens of JSON schemas are injected into the context window *before* any user input. This overhead occurs even if the tools are never used.

This translates to a significant cost. For a Claude Pro subscription, this pre-injection alone could cost $1,764 annually, effectively paying to load JSON descriptions of tools that might remain unused.

Beyond initial connection, MCP also adds substantial overhead to tool call results. A 38-character content response can be wrapped in 47 characters of JSON, meaning 55% of result tokens are pure overhead.

This token bloat becomes critical in complex AI agent workflows, multi-turn reasoning, and long debugging sessions. When context windows are already strained, these injected schemas can cause conversations to "fall off a cliff."

Anthropic, MCP's designer, has shown that token consumption can drop by 98.7% (from 150,000 to 2,000) by *not* loading tool schemas into context. Their solution suggests letting the model write code to call tools at runtime.

Cloudflare further demonstrated this inefficiency, reducing their 2,500-endpoint API's schema from 1.17 million tokens to just 1,000 by exposing only two functions: search and execute. This drastic reduction highlights the architectural flaw.

Despite its popularity, with 97 million monthly downloads, MCP's design is fundamentally questioned. Its widespread adoption is attributed to being first, backed by major players, and a lack of ready alternatives at the time.

The core issue isn't the protocol itself, but the implementation pattern: forcing models to load every tool schema into context at startup. This is akin to a carpenter reading every manual before picking up a hammer.

The proposed fix is not a new protocol, but a smarter proxy layer. This layer, exemplified by the 'mcptoon' CLI proxy, would load schemas on demand and strip unnecessary JSON wrapping, allowing the model to focus on the task.
